column4: The verse first requires Scripture holders to explain the revelation to people and not conceal it, then says they threw it “فَنَبَذُوهُ وَرَاءَ ظُهُورِهِمْ.” This is the source section’s root ظ ه ر in its dictionary sense of putting something behind one’s back and forgetting it, set against public explanation.
A group given Scripture discards God’s Book “وَرَاءَ ظُهُورِهِمْ”; this is the source section’s ظ ه ر image of putting away and forgetting the very book that should be kept in mind.

Shuʿayb rebukes his people for putting God behind their backs and disregarding Him (“وَرَاءَكُمْ ظِهْرِيًّا”). This gives the source section’s ظ ه ر dictionary extension a lived case: they treat God's command as forgettable.

The recipient is given his record “وَرَاءَ ظَهْرِهِ.” The source section’s back-as-forgetting image turns into its judgmental reversal: the book once put aside returns behind the bearer as an unavoidable record.
The promise “سَنُقْرِئُكَ فَلَا تَنسَىٰ” directly reverses the source section’s forgotten thing put behind one’s back: God will recite to the Prophet and he will not forget.
Here al-dhikr is sent down and God is its ḥāfiẓ. This joins the source section’s dictionary senses of ذ ك ر as scripture and keeping something in memory to an explicit promise of preservation.

The verse calls the revelation al-dhikr and gives the Prophet the task “لِتُبَيِّنَ لِلنَّاسِ.” It brings together the source section’s ذ ك ر as prophetic scripture and ش ر ح as making something clear to people.

The Prophet is told not to move his tongue hastily with revelation, “لَا تُحَرِّكْ بِهِۦ لِسَانَكَ.” This concretely meets the source section’s dictionary image of carrying Qur’an on the tongue while preserving it.

The next ayah assigns the collection and recitation of revelation to God (“جَمْعَهُۥ وَقُرْءَانَهُۥ”). It completes 75:16’s tongue-and-retention scene with the source section’s concern for what is kept and recited.

After the promise of collection in 75:17, this ayah tells the Prophet to follow the recitation when it is recited. Its own contribution is the audible transmission that corresponds to the source section’s Qur’an carried on the tongue.

After collection and recitation (75:17–18), God also undertakes its bayān. The source section’s dictionary branch of ش ر ح means explaining/opening; this ayah places clarification after the received recitation.

The verse says those entrusted with the Torah were to guard God’s Book (“ٱسْتُحْفِظُوا۟ مِن كِتَٰبِ ٱللَّهِ”). This is a concrete human counterpart to the source section’s dictionary sense of شرح as guarding/preserving and ذ ك ر as a prophetic book.

The stated purpose of sending the Book is that the Prophet clarify what people differ about. This directly parallels the source section’s ش ر ح dictionary sense of opening what is closed, now applied to revealed teaching.

The verse says God knows the unseen and “فَلَا يُظْهِرُ عَلَىٰ غَيْبِهِۦٓ أَحَدًا.” The source section’s root ظ ه ر includes a hidden thing becoming manifest; this ayah sets a boundary on who can disclose the unseen.

Following 72:26, this ayah specifies the exception: a messenger whom God approves, with guards before and behind him. Its own contribution is to make the source section’s disclosure boundary selective rather than absolute.

The next ayah explains that the messengers must convey their Lord’s messages and that God encompasses what they have. It completes 72:27’s guarded exception with the public conveyance that the source section associates with making the hidden manifest.

“فَٱذْكُرُونِىٓ أَذْكُرْكُمْ” makes remembrance reciprocal. It directly enacts the source section’s ذ ك ر sense of remembering, while adding that the remembrance of God and people answers one another.

The Prophet complains that his people took this Qur’an as “مَهْجُورًا,” abandoned. This is a specific communal counterpart to the source section’s contrast between what is cast behind the back and what is retained and raised as dhikr.

The verse says a covenant-breaking group forgot a portion of what they had been reminded of (“نَسُوا۟ حَظًّا مِّمَّا ذُكِّرُوا۟ بِهِ”). It gives the source section’s remembered/forgotten contrast a concrete scriptural setting.

About another group, the verse likewise says they forgot a portion of what they were reminded of. This is a separate instance of the source section’s central movement from reminder to loss from memory.

Adam is said to have forgotten the covenant previously made with him (“فَنَسِىَ”). This gives the source section’s forgetting branch a specific instance where a prior divine word fails to remain held in mind.

The verse’s condition is turning away from “ذِكْرِى.” It contrasts the source section’s raised remembrance with deliberate refusal of remembrance, and names the consequence that follows in its context.

Satan makes a people forget the remembrance of God (“أَنسَىٰهُمْ ذِكْرَ ٱللَّهِ”). This is a direct counter-image to the source section’s preserved and raised dhikr: remembrance is displaced rather than retained.
The warning not to forget God, followed by God making them forget themselves, develops the source section’s memory/forgetting axis as a loss that alters self-knowledge, not merely a missed word.

This verse condemns concealing revealed proofs and guidance after they were made clear to people in Scripture. It directly meets the source section’s movement from what is hidden to what is explained and disclosed.
The verse condemns those who conceal what God sent down of the Book. It makes concealment a concrete refusal of the source section’s written dhikr becoming available to people.

In this rebuke about Moses’ Book, people make it into separate sheets, show some, and conceal much. The scene directly stages the source section’s paired movement between a book being exposed and kept hidden.

The verse places secret speech beside speech uttered openly, and what is hidden by night beside what moves about by day. It concretely echoes the source section’s hidden/manifest axis across both word and presence.

Whether people conceal their speech or say it aloud, God knows what is within the breasts. This is a close parallel to the source section’s passage from hidden to spoken, while locating knowledge of both with God.

The Prophet is commanded to convey what was sent down to him. This is a concrete public-spreading counterpart to the source section’s dictionary branch of ر ف ع as disseminating and making something manifest.
The sent-down Book is described as containing the people’s dhikr (“كِتَابًا فِيهِ ذِكْرُكُمْ”). This directly meets the source section’s dictionary sense that prophetic scripture itself is dhikr.

Moses and Aaron are given the Criterion, light, and a dhikr for the God-fearing. It supplies a second prophetic-book instance for the source section’s dictionary claim that every prophetic book is dhikr.
The verse explicitly calls the sent-down revelation “ذِكْرٌ مُّبَارَكٌ.” It directly supports the source section’s dictionary sense of ذ ك ر as a prophetic book, here blessed and sent down.

The Qur’an is called a dhikr for the Prophet and his people, who will be questioned about it. This makes the source section’s book-as-dhikr a public relation between recited revelation and its audience.

The Qur’an is made easy upon the Prophet’s tongue so people may remember (“بِلِسَانِكَ لَعَلَّهُمْ يَتَذَكَّرُونَ”). This closely joins the source section’s tongue-carried Qur’an to its account of remembrance.

The event is made a reminder, “وَتَعِيَهَآ أُذُنٌ وَٰعِيَةٌ,” so an attentive ear retains it. This gives bodily form to the source section’s dictionary definition of dhikr as keeping something in memory.
The passage calls the recited message a reminder (“تَذْكِرَةٌ”), matching the source section’s dictionary sense of a tadhkira as that by which something is remembered.
The next ayah says whoever wills may remember it (“ذَكَرَهُۥ”). It completes 80:11’s reminder with the act of retaining it, as in the source section’s account of dhikr.
The reminder of 80:11–12 is in honored pages (“صُحُفٍ مُّكَرَّمَةٍ”). This gives a written form to the source section’s dictionary sense of dhikr as prophetic scripture.

The pages of 80:13 are “مَّرْفُوعَةٍ مُّطَهَّرَةٍ.” The same source-section root ر ف ع that can mean spreading or making manifest is used here for pages physically elevated; that difference sharpens the image rather than equating the senses.

The elevated pages of 80:13–14 are in the hands of scribes. This completes the passage’s physical transmission of written reminder, alongside the source section’s parallel image of Qur’an carried on the tongue.
The Qur’an is located in a preserved tablet (“فِى لَوْحٍ مَّحْفُوظٍ”). This concretely joins the source section’s book-as-dhikr and keeping/guarding senses to a preserved written record.
A messenger recites purified pages. The verse stages the source section’s two forms of carrying revelation: an inscribed book and its movement on a reader’s tongue.

The pages recited in 98:2 contain upright writings. This ayah’s contribution is to identify the content of the spoken pages, corresponding to the source section’s dictionary sense of prophetic books as dhikr.

The passage says the faithful spirit brought the revelation; 26:194 locates it on the Prophet’s heart and 26:195 calls it a clear Arabic tongue. This begins a concrete hidden-to-spoken route parallel to the source section’s heart-memory and tongue-carried Qur’an.

This ayah locates the revelation on the Prophet’s heart so he can warn, completing 26:193’s arrival and anticipating the clear Arabic tongue of 26:195. It closely parallels the source section’s memorization in the heart before speech.

The next ayah names a clear Arabic tongue (“بِلِسَانٍ عَرَبِيٍّ مُّبِينٍ”). It completes 26:193–194’s movement from revelation to heart to speech, like the source section’s Qur’an borne on the tongue.

The verse describes those given the Book reciting it with its due recitation. This is a specific practice of carrying scripture in speech, as in the source section’s dictionary image of Qur’an borne on the tongue.

When Qur’an is recited, listeners are told to hear it and attend in silence. The ayah supplies the hearer’s side of the source section’s spoken dhikr, making public utterance something received and retained.

The Qur’an is divided for people to recite it over time, with measured recitation. This directly parallels the source section’s image of scripture carried by the reader’s tongue and made public in speech.
The Prophet is told to recite the Qur’an in measured recitation. This is a specific oral practice corresponding to the source section’s dictionary image of bearing the Qur’an on the tongue.
The Qur’an is made easy in the Prophet’s tongue for warning and good news. This directly stages the source section’s tongue-carried revelation as speech that reaches others.

The disbelievers urge one another not to listen to the Qur’an and to make noise during its recitation. This is a specific obstruction of the source section’s word moving aloud and being heard or remembered.

When Qur’an is recited, a hidden barrier is placed between the Prophet and those who deny the Hereafter (“حِجَابًا مَّسْتُورًا”). The recitation becomes concealed from its intended listeners, reversing the source section’s movement from hidden to manifest.

The next ayah describes coverings over hearts and deafness in ears when the Lord alone is mentioned. It completes 17:45’s barrier by showing why the spoken reminder does not reach or move its hearers.

Believers are asked whether the time has come for their hearts to humble themselves at God’s remembrance and the truth sent down. This links the source section’s remembrance to the inward retention and response of its hearers.

When reminded of God’s signs, believers fall prostrate and glorify Him rather than act arrogantly. This supplies a concrete receptive response to reminder, in contrast to the source section’s images of putting a word aside.

The Book is sent down as blessed so people may reflect on its verses and those of understanding take reminder. This directly joins written revelation to the source section’s dictionary senses of book-as-dhikr and recalling through it.

The Prophet is to warn by the Qur’an those who follow the reminder and fear the unseen. This makes the source section’s dhikr a recited warning that a hearer follows, rather than merely a word retained privately.
The Prophet is told to remind by the Qur’an whoever fears God’s warning. This directly connects the source section’s book-as-dhikr to the public act of reminding through recitation.
The command “remind” is justified because reminder benefits believers. It concretely extends the source section’s dhikr from preserved memory to speech that renews memory in an audience.

After the account of Noah’s people, the verse says the Qur’an has been made easy for remembrance and asks who will remember. This directly joins the source section’s remembrance and repeated reminder to a recited scripture.

After the account of ʿĀd, the same refrain says the Qur’an is made easy for remembrance and asks who will remember. The repeated occurrence shows the source section’s “many remembrances” sense enacted across distinct warnings.
After the account of Thamud, this refrain again makes the Qur’an easy for remembrance. Its placement after another people’s fate concretely repeats the source section’s reminder/retention relation.
After Lot’s people, the refrain again asks who will remember the Qur’an made easy for remembrance. This is a separate contextual instance of the source section’s repeated dhikr.
The Prophet is told to remind when reminder benefits. This directly parallels the source section’s dictionary description of tadhkira as what enables remembering, now as a prophetic address.
The next ayah says the one who fears will remember (“سَيَذَّكَّرُ مَن يَخْشَىٰ”). It completes 87:9’s reminder with the listener’s retention, matching the source section’s account of dhikr.
The one most wretched avoids that reminder, reversing the remembering listener of 87:10. The pair makes visible the source section’s divide between what is held in mind and what is put away.
The passage calls the Qur’an a reminder. This directly meets the source section’s dictionary sense of dhikr as scripture and a reminder, before 74:55 specifies a hearer’s response.
The following ayah says whoever wills may remember it. It completes 74:54’s reminder with the act of keeping it in mind, as in the source section’s definition of dhikr.
The Qur’an is described as a reminder to all worlds. This supports the source section’s specific dictionary sense of prophetic scripture itself as dhikr, with a universal audience.
The Prophet is commanded to remind, and identified as a reminder-giver. This directly parallels the source section’s account of dhikr as something that brings a thing back to mind.
The next ayah says the Prophet is not a controller over them. It bounds the reminder-command of 88:21: the word can be made public, but its hearers cannot be compelled to retain it.

The next ayah says they will not remember unless God wills. It adds a limit to the reminder and willing response in 74:54–55, resonating with the source section’s distinction between what is recalled and what remains hidden.

After recounting earlier events, the verse says God has given the Prophet a reminder from Himself. This is a specific case of revealed narrative serving as dhikr, as in the source section’s book-and-memory sense.
The verses recited to the Prophet are called wise remembrance. This is a concrete instance of recited revelation as dhikr, corresponding to the source section’s book and spoken-word senses.
Whenever a new reminder comes to the people, they listen playfully. It shows the source section’s remembrance reaching the ear without being seriously retained.
Whoever turns away from the remembrance of the Merciful is assigned a companion. This is a specific refusal of the source section’s remembered word, with a consequence attached to turning away.

Those who disbelieve in the Reminder when it comes to them are condemned, though it is a mighty Book. This concretely stages rejection of the source section’s book-as-dhikr when it becomes present to its audience.

The sent-down Book is described as repeated and mutually reinforcing, and its hearers’ hearts soften toward remembrance of God. The bridge to the source section’s “many remembrances” gloss is interpretive: here repetition describes the scripture and its effect.

The Qur’an gives every kind of example so that people may remember. This connects the source section’s dictionary sense of tadhkira, a means by which something is remembered, to a particular teaching method in revelation.

The verse identifies the Qur’an as a reminder and invites whoever wills to take a way to the Lord. It concretely joins remembered revelation to a hearer’s response, as in the source section’s account of dhikr.
The Prophet is told to remind and not to be a soothsayer or mad. This is a specific prophetic use of the reminder-word developed in the source section, though the surrounding polemic is distinct.

Abraham says God knows what they conceal and declare. This is a specific but indirect parallel to the source section’s hidden/open axis; it concerns human speech before God, not scripture’s disclosure.
God knows what people conceal and make manifest. This is a specific but indirect parallel to the source section’s hidden/manifest relation, applied to divine knowledge of human acts.

The verse says God knows people’s secret and public dealings. This is a plausible but broad parallel to the source section’s hidden/manifest axis; it describes divine knowledge, not disclosure of scripture.
Believers are warned not to let wealth or children distract them from God’s remembrance. This is a specific rival to the source section’s keeping dhikr in mind: worldly attention can displace it.
The verse forbids mixing truth with falsehood and concealing the truth while knowing it. This is a specific boundary against the source section’s movement from hidden teaching to clear public speech.

The verse challenges Scripture holders who conceal truth while knowing it. It is a concrete reversal of the source section’s explanation-and-disclosure movement, though it does not use the back image.

The Messenger brings light and a clear Book, making clear much of what Scripture holders had concealed. This directly develops the source section’s passage from hidden teaching to explanation and public disclosure.

The verse calls the sent-down Book a clarification for all things and guidance. This directly parallels the source section’s dictionary sense of ش ر ح as making something clear, now stated as the Book’s purpose.

The Prophet is told to recite what has been revealed from his Lord’s Book, whose words cannot be altered. This joins the source section’s Qur’an-on-the-tongue image to the preservation of the recited text.
The verse calls the reminder for the Prophet’s generation and for those before them. It directly supports the source section’s dictionary claim that the books of earlier prophets are dhikr as well.

The verse says the Word has been conveyed to the people so that they may remember. It directly meets the source section’s account of a word spread outward and dhikr as what brings something back to mind.

The verse asks whether it is not enough that the Book was sent down and is recited to them, and calls it mercy and reminder for believers. It concretely joins the source section’s Book-as-dhikr to public recitation.

The Prophet is not taught poetry; the revelation is a reminder and a clear Qur’an. This specifies the source section’s spoken dhikr as clear revealed speech, and distinguishes it from another kind of utterance.
The verse says there is a reminder for one who has a heart or gives ear while present. This connects the source section’s memory held in the heart with its spoken word that reaches a listener.
The verse says the Merciful taught al-bayān. The source section explicitly gives al-bayān as the dictionary wording for ش ر ح; this ayah names that clarifying expression as something taught.
The ayah says a reminder may benefit its hearer. It directly matches the source section’s dictionary definition of tadhkira as what enables remembering.
A group of jinn listen to the Qur’an, then return to their people as warners. This concretely stages the source section’s word carried aloud and disseminated from one audience to another.

The next ayah reports the jinn identifying what they heard as a Book sent down after Moses and guiding to truth. Its own contribution is to name the heard recitation as scripture, matching the source section’s prophetic-book sense of dhikr.
The jinn then urge their people to answer God’s caller and believe. This completes the transmission begun in 46:29–30 with the response sought from those who hear the message.
A group of jinn hear the recitation and repeat that they have heard a wondrous Qur’an. This directly stages the source section’s spoken word becoming something an audience remembers and reports.

The next ayah says that the Qur’an guides to the right way and that the listeners believe in it. It gives the response to the hearing scene in 72:1, showing the public recitation retained as guidance.
The Qur’an is described as a reminder for those who fear. This is a direct instance of the source section’s dictionary sense of prophetic scripture as dhikr.
The verse says people of God should teach the Book and study it. This is a specific practice of keeping and transmitting scripture, though it does not use the source section’s word dhikr.

The signs are explained in varied ways so that the message may be made clear to people who know. This parallels the source section’s movement from what is closed to what is explained, though the ayah does not use the root ش ر ح.

This Qur’an relates to the Children of Israel much of what they differ about. That gives a specific interpretive parallel to the source section’s dictionary sense of ش ر ح as explanation, although this ayah says it recounts rather than using the source term.
The Merciful is said to have taught the Qur’an. This is a specific instance of the prophetic Book as taught discourse, corresponding to the source section’s dictionary sense of dhikr as scripture.
The successful person remembers the name of his Lord and prays. This is a concrete instance of the source section’s ذ ك ر as keeping a thing in mind and letting it be present in utterance.
The opening command is to read in the name of the Lord. This gives a specific recitation scene for the source section’s image of a reader bearing Qur’an on the tongue.

A group hear God’s words and then deliberately distort them after understanding. This is a specific reversal of the source section’s preserved and clarified word: hearing and carrying revelation can also be followed by deliberate alteration.

Some twist their tongues with the Book so listeners think their speech belongs to Scripture, though it does not. This is a concrete misuse of the source section’s tongue-carried Book image, false public transmission rather than faithful recitation.
The ayah says God taught by the pen. Alongside the reading command in 96:1, it supplies the written side of the source section’s paired images of remembered scripture and Qur’an carried in speech.
